interactions: Ibuprofen with dexamethasone: additive risk of gastrointestinal ulceration and bleeding; ibuprofen also impairs platelet function. Avoid the combination.
Sertraline with ibuprofen: SSRIs reduce platelet serotonin uptake and add to NSAID-related bleeding risk.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Irregular heterogeneously enhancing left temporal mass (3.8 cm) without a classic ring, with restricted diffusion at the enhancing margin, central non-enhancing areas, vasogenic oedema, 2 mm midline shift and extension toward the insula
action_criteria.label: Order MRI brain with and without gadolinium (tumour protocol with DWI, FLAIR, post-contrast T1) to characterise the left temporal lesion, define mass effect and plan surgery
action_criteria.rationale: Contrast-enhanced MRI with diffusion and FLAIR is the standard imaging for a suspected diffuse glioma: it defines the enhancing target, the oedema and the mass effect, and plans the surgical approach (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: rCBV ratio up to 3.8 in the enhancing component, supporting a high-grade neoplasm and the sampling target
action_criteria.label: Order MR perfusion (DSC) to assess tumour vascularity and target the most aggressive region for tissue sampling
action_criteria.rationale: Elevated rCBV supports a high-grade neoplasm and identifies the region to sample; it does not grade or exclude, tissue decides (Law 2003).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Cho/NAA 5.3 with lipid-lactate in the enhancing component; borderline choline in the peritumoral region
action_criteria.label: Order MR spectroscopy (1H-MRS) to characterise the metabolic profile of the lesion
action_criteria.rationale: Elevated choline with reduced NAA and lipid-lactate supports a high-grade neoplasm; it does not establish the diagnosis, tissue does (Bulik 2013).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Intermittent left temporal polymorphic delta slowing without epileptiform discharges; the spells remain uncharacterised
action_criteria.label: Order an EEG to characterise the brief staring spells
action_criteria.rationale: The staring spells are unwitnessed and uncertain; an EEG helps decide whether they are seizures, which would indicate antiseizure treatment (AIOM). EEG does not diagnose the tumour.

action_criteria.label: Order CT chest, abdomen and pelvis with contrast if a solitary metastasis remains on the differential

action_criteria.rationale: A neurosurgical procedure and corticosteroids are anticipated; platelets, coagulation, electrolytes and glucose must be known before either.

action_criteria.label: Order functional MRI to map language and motor cortex relative to the lesion before resection
action_criteria.rationale: The lesion lies close to Wernicke area in the dominant hemisphere; functional mapping plans a maximal safe resection (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Arcuate fasciculus displaced about 6 mm from the superior margin; Meyer loop within the temporal-stem oedema

action_criteria.rationale: The lesion and its oedema lie close to the left arcuate fasciculus and Meyer loop; tractography plans a maximal safe resection (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Integrated diagnosis Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, CNS WHO grade 4 with IDH1 R132H negative, IDH1/IDH2 wildtype on sequencing, ATRX retained and MGMT promoter methylated
action_criteria.label: Obtain tissue by maximal safe resection of the left temporal lesion, or stereotactic biopsy if resection is not safely feasible, for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis with IDH1 R132H immunohistochemistry, IDH1/IDH2 sequencing, ATRX immunohistochemistry and MGMT promoter methylation
action_criteria.rationale: Surgery is the first option for a resectable glioma and should be as extensive as safely possible (AIOM Q1; EANO 2021). Only tissue establishes the integrated diagnosis and the molecular results that select treatment.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Stop ibuprofen (bleeding risk with dexamethasone and sertraline); watch mood if levetiracetam is used

action_criteria.rationale: Dexamethasone and possibly levetiracetam will be started; the current medicines and allergy are checked before prescribing.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform a lumbar puncture: the left temporal mass causes midline shift and temporal horn effacement, and the pressure gradient risks herniation.
Do not start radiotherapy, temozolomide or other tumour-directed therapy before the integrated tissue diagnosis is established.
Do not start therapeutic anticoagulation without a clear thromboembolic indication, given the planned neurosurgery and bleeding risk.
required_recommendations: Refer urgently to neurosurgery for maximal safe resection of the left temporal lesion, with preoperative functional MRI and DTI tractography and intraoperative mapping, with stereotactic biopsy if resection is not safely feasible; send the specimen for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis (WHO CNS5).

Start dexamethasone for symptomatic vasogenic oedema (for example 4 mg every 6 to 8 hours after a loading dose when mass effect is marked) at the lowest effective dose, with glucose monitoring and gastric protection, and taper after surgery.
Characterise the brief staring spells with an EEG; start levetiracetam only if they are judged to be seizures, not as prophylaxis.
Stop as-needed ibuprofen before neurosurgery and while on dexamethasone (platelet inhibition and gastrointestinal bleeding risk, increased by sertraline); use paracetamol for headache.

After the integrated diagnosis, refer to the neuro-oncology multidisciplinary team; for glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, at age 52 with KPS 80, the standard is radiotherapy 60 Gy in 30 fractions with concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide (Stupp 2005; EANO 2021), from which the MGMT-methylated tumour is expected to benefit most.

clinical_pearls: Not all glioblastomas present with the classic ring-enhancing pattern — irregular heterogeneous enhancement can also represent high-grade glioma, especially when perfusion and spectroscopy show aggressive features

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Deborah Marston is a 52-year-old right-handed woman and high school English teacher who was referred to the neurology service by her primary care physician after two months of progressive word-finding difficulty and personality changes noted by her family. Her husband reports that the first noticeable change was approximately two months ago when she began misplacing common words during dinner conversations — something highly unusual for a woman who has taught literature for 24 years and has always been exceptionally articulate. Initially, the family attributed this to stress and fatigue related to the school year. Over the following weeks, however, the word-finding difficulty became more prominent and was accompanied by a subtle but unmistakable change in her personality. Her husband describes her as becoming increasingly apathetic and emotionally flat, quite unlike her previously warm and expressive demeanor. She stopped initiating plans with friends, which was out of character, and on several occasions became unusually irritable over trivial matters. Approximately six weeks ago, she began experiencing headaches that she described as a dull, persistent pressure predominantly on the left side, worse in the morning upon waking and sometimes associated with mild nausea. She attributed these to tension headaches and increased her use of over-the-counter ibuprofen without significant relief. Three weeks ago, her daughter noticed that she struggled to help with a crossword puzzle, something the two of them had enjoyed together for years, and that she seemed to stare blankly for brief moments. There has been no witnessed seizure activity, though the family is uncertain whether these brief staring episodes could represent seizures. She denies any visual changes, though on directed questioning she admits that she occasionally has difficulty seeing things on her right side when driving, leading her to stop driving two weeks ago. She has lost approximately 4 kg of weight over the past two months without intentional dieting, which she attributes to reduced appetite. Her primary care physician obtained an outpatient non-contrast CT of the head, which showed a left temporal hypodensity with surrounding oedema and slight midline shift, prompting urgent referral and admission.
